claim: phiC31 site-specific recombination mediated by plasmid transfection achieved ~20% integration efficiency in Drosophila S2R+ PT5 cells without selection.
source: Integration efficiency, inferred through flow cytometry (Figure 1B), suggested that phiC31-mediated cassette exchange occurred in ~20% of the cells (even without accounting for incomplete transfection), 123-fold more than the background illegitimate recombination rate observed without phiC31 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 1B, which quantified GFP-positive cells after phiC31-mediated recombination.

claim: phiC31-mediated integration efficiency was 123-fold higher than background illegitimate recombination rate without phiC31.
source: Integration efficiency, inferred through flow cytometry (Figure 1B), suggested that phiC31-mediated cassette exchange occurred in ~20% of the cells (even without accounting for incomplete transfection), 123-fold more than the background illegitimate recombination rate observed without phiC31 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative flow cytometry data showing integration with and without phiC31 helper plasmid.

claim: pLib6.4 with separated attB sites allowed ~40 fold greater integration efficiency than traditional Drosophila attB40 vectors with adjacent attB sites.
source: Interestingly, pLib6.4, which contains separated attB sites flanking the DNA sequence to be integrated, allowed ~40 fold greater integration efficiency than traditional Drosophila attB40 vectors such as pCa4B (Markstein et al., 2008), in which the attB sites are adjacent and require integration of the entire plasmid (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison data between pLib6.4 and pCa4B vectors, though the data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: PT5/Cas9 cells without induction were capable of editing nearly 50% of Dredd alleles.
source: In combination with an sgRNA targeting the nonessential gene Dredd, PT5/Cas9 cells without induction were capable of editing nearly 50% of Dredd alleles, which was higher than that achieved by repeated rounds of transient transfection with a SpCas9 expression plasmid (Figure 1C) and not improved by copper induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by T7E1 editing efficiency assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Constitutive Cas9 showed more selective reduction of Rho1 or Diap1 sgRNAs than inducible Cas9.
source: Surprisingly, a comparison of dropout efficiencies between the inducible and constitutive Cas9 platforms showed more selective reduction of Rho1 or Diap1 sgRNAs with constitutive rather than inducible Cas9, most likely due to the lower overall editing efficiency from intein-Cas9 as previously reported (Liu et al., 2016) (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative dropout efficiency data shown in Figure 1G and supplementary figures, with citation to previous work on intein-Cas9 efficiency.

claim: 45 days of passaging is optimal for monitoring sgRNA dropout in pooled screens.
source: Monitoring Rho1 or Diap1-targeted sgRNAs in the screen pools 30, 45, or 60 days post-transfection showed that 45 days of passaging is optimal (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data comparing sgRNA dropout at different time points shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The genome-wide sgRNA library contains 85,558 sgRNAs targeting 13,928 Drosophila genes.
source: The top ranked 6–8 sgRNAs per gene (85,558 in total) were chosen and synthesized together on a microarray chip with non-targeting and intergenic negative controls, harvested by PCR, and cloned into pLib6.4 using published methods (Gilbert et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text describing library construction, with citation to the cloning method.

claim: 1235 genes were essential for cell fitness at a false-discovery rate of 5% in Drosophila S2R+ cells under basal growth conditions.
source: Under basal growth conditions, 1235 genes were essential for cell fitness at a false-discovery rate of 5%, representing the highest-resolution fitness gene set yet assembled for Drosophila, including 407 genes which likely duplicated along the vertebrate lineage and whose orthologs were underrepresented in human CRISPR screens.
evidence: The claim is supported by genome-wide CRISPR screen data analyzed using MAGeCK and FDR calculations.

claim: The 1235 fitness genes represent the highest-resolution fitness gene set yet assembled for Drosophila.
source: Under basal growth conditions, 1235 genes were essential for cell fitness at a false-discovery rate of 5%, representing the highest-resolution fitness gene set yet assembled for Drosophila, including 407 genes which likely duplicated along the vertebrate lineage and whose orthologs were underrepresented in human CRISPR screens.
evidence: The claim is asserted based on comparison with previous Drosophila screens, particularly RNAi screens.

claim: 407 fitness genes likely duplicated along the vertebrate lineage and their orthologs were underrepresented in human CRISPR screens.
source: Under basal growth conditions, 1235 genes were essential for cell fitness at a false-discovery rate of 5%, representing the highest-resolution fitness gene set yet assembled for Drosophila, including 407 genes which likely duplicated along the vertebrate lineage and whose orthologs were underrepresented in human CRISPR screens.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis between Drosophila and human CRISPR screens using ortholog mapping.

claim: Sequential biological replicates of the genome-wide screen showed good gene-level correlation with Pearson's r = 0.65.
source: We used MAGeCK (Li et al., 2014) maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to compute fitness Z-scores for each gene from the log2 fold-changes of individual sgRNAs, which yielded good gene-level correlation between sequential biological replicates (Figure 2C; Pearson's r = 0.65).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C using MAGeCK MLE analysis.

claim: Fitness genes were highly enriched for genes with any expression level of RPKM > 1.
source: Because all true fitness genes must be expressed as mRNA, fitness scores were compared with gene expression from S2R+ cells (Celniker et al., 2009) as an orthogonal validation of the CRISPR results (Figure 2D). Fitness genes were highly enriched for genes with any expression level of RPKM > 1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of CRISPR fitness scores with RNAseq expression data from modENCODE.

claim: Re-analyzed RNAi-based fitness gene set had a far higher FDR compared with pooled CRISPR screen results, allowing the discovery of only 145 fitness genes at an FDR of 5%.
source: We re-analyzed a genome-wide RNAi viability screen in S2R+ cells (Boutros et al., 2004) and removed double-stranded RNA designs with predicted off-targets, which significantly lowered the FDR of the RNAi screen (see Materials and methods). Nevertheless, compared with pooled CRISPR screen results, the re-analyzed RNAi-based fitness gene set still had a far higher FDR, allowing the discovery of only 145 fitness genes at an FDR of 5% or incurring 44% FDR with a fitness gene set of 1235 genes (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by re-analysis of published RNAi data and comparison with CRISPR results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CRISPR was better able than RNAi to identify significant fractions of the mitochondrial ribosome, aminoacyl-tRNA ligases, RNA polymerase II, basal transcription factors, RNA exosome, or the replication fork at low FDR.
source: Whereas CRISPR and RNAi were both able to detect cytoplasmic ribosomal or proteasomal genes, CRISPR was better able than RNAi to identify significant fractions of the mitochondrial ribosome, aminoacyl-tRNA ligases, RNA polymerase II, basal transcription factors, RNA exosome, or the replication fork at low FDR (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC curve analysis comparing CRISPR and RNAi detection of conserved macromolecular complexes shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Neither CRISPR nor RNAi detected peroxisome genes, consistent with the observation that cell lines lacking peroxisomes grow normally.
source: As a control, neither method detected peroxisome genes, consistent with the observation that cell lines lacking peroxisomes grow normally (Goldfischer et al., 1973) (data not shown) (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative results in both CRISPR and RNAi screens, with citation to previous work on peroxisome-deficient cell lines.

claim: The fly CRISPR screen had similar sensitivity to genome-wide screens in human cell-lines performed with similar reagent number (GeCKO v2 screens) when compared against top RNAi hits.
source: A technical comparison of CRISPR screens in humans and fly cells indicated that the method performs similarly in both systems. First, the fly screen had similar sensitivity (true-positive rate at 5% FDR) to genome-wide screens in human cell-lines performed with similar reagent number (GeCKO v2 screens) when compared against top RNAi hits (Sanjana et al., 2014) (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of true-positive rates between fly and human CRISPR screens shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The position matrix for optimal sgRNA design in Drosophila shows complementary nucleotide biases at 15/21 positions and is broadly consistent with human CRISPR screens.
source: By comparing sgRNAs that dropped out versus those that failed to dropout for known essential genes, we were able to compute a probability-based position matrix for optimal sgRNA design in Drosophila (Figure 2H). The position matrix shows complementary nucleotide biases at 15/21 positions and is broadly consistent with human CRISPR screens (Doench et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by position matrix analysis shown in Figure 2H and comparison with published human sgRNA design rules.

claim: Out of the first position of the PAM sequence and the 8 bp seed region before the PAM sequence, 5 of 9 positions are fully consistent while 2 of 9 position are partially consistent with the Doench score.
source: Specifically, out of the first position of the PAM sequence and the 8 bp seed region before the PAM sequence, 5 of 9 positions are fully consistent while 2 of 9 position are partially consistent with the Doench score (Doench et al., 2016) (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by detailed comparison of the Drosophila position matrix with the Doench score shown in Figure 2H.

claim: CRISPR in Drosophila shows no detectable bias towards CNA genes for 97% of the genome.
source: Copy number has been shown to correlate with the CRISPR viability score in some mammalian CRISPR screens, presumably due to induction of greater DNA damage foci for copy-number-amplified (CNA) loci, creating spurious fitness calls (Meyers et al., 2017). By contrast, we find that CRISPR in Drosophila shows no detectable bias towards CNA genes for 97% of the genome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of copy number effects shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, with citation to mammalian CRISPR screen studies.

claim: Genes with extreme CNA of 8 or more copies (3% of genes) exhibited a bias of ~1.8 fold in the CRISPR screen, but the magnitude of this bias was similar to that seen in an RNAi screen for the same genes.
source: Interestingly, genes with extreme CNA of 8 or more copies (3% of genes) exhibited a bias of ~1.8 fold in the CRISPR screen, but the magnitude of this bias was similar to that seen in an RNAi screen for the same genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that CNA genes in Drosophila cells are enriched for fitness essentiality.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of CNA effects in CRISPR and RNAi screens shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Copy-number correction had no detectable effect on FDR, true-positive rate, or enrichment of major macromolecular complexes.
source: Finally, copy-number correction had no detectable effect on FDR, true-positive rate, or enrichment of major macromolecular complexes (not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated based on analysis that was performed but not shown in the manuscript.

claim: At 5% FDR, ~17% of cell-essential genes overlapped with whole-fly essential genes.
source: Next, we compared CRISPR hits to fly genes with lethal alleles annotated in FlyBase after removing genes for which no allele has yet been constructed. At 5% FDR,~17% of cell-essential genes overlapped with whole-fly essential genes (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of CRISPR hits with FlyBase lethal allele annotations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The overlap between cell-essential and whole-fly essential genes is in a similar range as knockout mouse viability compared with mouse cell-line fitness essentiality (where the overlap is ~27%).
source: This overlap is in a similar range as knockout mouse viability compared with mouse cell-line fitness essentiality (where the overlap is ~27%) (Bartha et al., 2018), and may represent different genetic requirements of whole animals versus cell lines or of germline versus somatic cells (Garcia-Bellido and Robbins, 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to mouse studies and inference about biological differences between organisms and cell lines.

claim: The fly fitness gene set partially but significantly overlaps with characterized fitness gene sets from yeast and human cells.
source: The fly fitness gene set partially but significantly overlaps with characterized fitness gene sets from yeast and human cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3C comparing fitness genes across species.

claim: An unbiased comparison of gene ontology terms between fly and human fitness genes displays a high degree of correlation (Pearson's r = 0.56).
source: Moreover, an unbiased comparison of gene ontology terms between fly and human fitness genes displays a high degree of correlation (Figure 3D; Pearson's r = 0.56).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis comparing fly and human fitness genes shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 35% of conserved human genes contain a fly-to-human paralog.
source: Using this framework, 35% of conserved human genes contain a fly-to-human paralog, and 407 fly fitness genes (at 5% FDR) are the orthologs of human genes containing at least one paralog.
evidence: The claim is supported by ortholog analysis using DIOPT to identify paralog relationships.

claim: 407 fly fitness genes (at 5% FDR) are the orthologs of human genes containing at least one paralog.
source: Using this framework, 35% of conserved human genes contain a fly-to-human paralog, and 407 fly fitness genes (at 5% FDR) are the orthologs of human genes containing at least one paralog.
evidence: The claim is supported by ortholog and paralog analysis using DIOPT and comparison with human CRISPR screens.

claim: There is a significant bias against detecting genes that are conserved in flies and have a paralog in the human genome in human cell-line CRISPR screens.
source: In the human cell-line CRISPR screen, we noted a significant bias against detecting genes that are conserved in flies and have a paralog in the human genome, and this bias was dramatically elevated for the human orthologs of fly fitness genes (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of human CRISPR screen data showing reduced detection of genes with fly-to-human paralogs, shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The paralog effect extended to a larger dataset generated by the cancer Dependency Map project, in which CRISPR screens were conducted in 436 human cell-lines.
source: Furthermore, this paralog effect extended to a larger dataset generated by the cancer Dependency Map project, in which CRISPR screens were conducted in 436 human cell-lines.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of DepMap data across 436 human cell lines showing similar paralog effects.

claim: Phenotypes have yet to be described for 303 of the 1235 fitness genes identified.
source: Although the Drosophila fitness genes we identified are enriched for characterized phenotypes and publication count relative to all genes (data not shown), phenotypes have yet to be described for 303 of them.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with existing phenotype annotations in databases.

claim: Among the 303 uncharacterized fitness genes, 251 have human orthologs.
source: Among these 303 genes, 251 have human orthologs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ortholog mapping analysis provided in Supplementary file 2.

claim: At 5% FDR, 62 fitness genes have no sequence similarity outside of flies using DIOPT.
source: At 5% FDR, we obtained 62 fitness genes with no sequence similarity outside of flies using DIOPT, and phenotype information exists regarding 25 of these (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ortholog analysis using DIOPT showing fly-specific genes.

claim: Fly-specific fitness genes include known cell-essential divergent genes such as ver and HipHop, which encode components of the telomerin complex, the putative functional analog of mammalian telomerase.
source: In confirmation of our methods, these included known cell-essential divergent genes such as ver and HipHop, which encode components of the telomerin complex, the putative functional analog of mammalian telomerase (Raffa et al., 2011; 2010), and Kmn1, Kmn2 and Spc105R, whose gene products may be structural anologs of Ndc80, and Mis12 complex components that interact with centromeric DNA, a proposed driver of speciation (Schittenhelm et al., 2007; 2009; Henikoff et al., 2001), as well as several chromatin-interacting proteins (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by identification of these genes in the screen and citation to previous characterization studies.

claim: Fly-specific fitness genes include Kmn1, Kmn2 and Spc105R, whose gene products may be structural analogs of Ndc80, and Mis12 complex components that interact with centromeric DNA.
source: In confirmation of our methods, these included known cell-essential divergent genes such as ver and HipHop, which encode components of the telomerin complex, the putative functional analog of mammalian telomerase (Raffa et al., 2011; 2010), and Kmn1, Kmn2 and Spc105R, whose gene products may be structural anologs of Ndc80, and Mis12 complex components that interact with centromeric DNA, a proposed driver of speciation (Schittenhelm et al., 2007; 2009; Henikoff et al., 2001), as well as several chromatin-interacting proteins (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by identification of these genes in the screen and citation to previous characterization studies.

claim: sgRNAs against aop conferred resistance specifically in the context of trametinib treatment.
source: We observed highly context-specific modes of resistance to each drug. As an illustration, sgRNAs against aop, a transcriptional repressor of the Ras/ERK/ETS pathway (Lai and Rubin, 1992), or the putative intracellular co-factor for rapamycin, FK506-bp2 (Thomson and Johnson, 2010), conferred resistance specifically in the context of tra or RAP, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by context-specific dropout data shown in Figure 4D and citation to previous work on aop function.

claim: sgRNAs against FK506-bp2 conferred resistance specifically in the context of rapamycin treatment.
source: We observed highly context-specific modes of resistance to each drug. As an illustration, sgRNAs against aop, a transcriptional repressor of the Ras/ERK/ETS pathway (Lai and Rubin, 1992), or the putative intracellular co-factor for rapamycin, FK506-bp2 (Thomson and Johnson, 2010), conferred resistance specifically in the context of tra or RAP, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by context-specific dropout data shown in Figure 4D and citation to previous work on FK506-bp2 function.

claim: Additional established context-specific pathway negative regulators emerged including PTP-ER, which inactivates Erk (rl).
source: Additional established context-specific pathway negative regulators emerged: PTP-ER, which inactivates Erk (rl) (Karim and Rubin, 1999) and Pi3K21B and Pten, which antagonize the activity of Pi3K92E (Weinkove et al., 1999; Huang et al., 1999; Goberdhan et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by identification of PTP-ER in the drug screens and citation to previous functional characterization.

claim: Additional established context-specific pathway negative regulators emerged including Pi3K21B and Pten, which antagonize the activity of Pi3K92E.
source: Additional established context-specific pathway negative regulators emerged: PTP-ER, which inactivates Erk (rl) (Karim and Rubin, 1999) and Pi3K21B and Pten, which antagonize the activity of Pi3K92E (Weinkove et al., 1999; Huang et al., 1999; Goberdhan et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by identification of Pi3K21B and Pten in the drug screens and citation to previous functional characterization.

claim: A network involved in photoreceptor cell differentiation scored most strongly as synergistically lethal with trametinib.
source: For instance, a network involved in photoreceptor cell differentiation scored most strongly as synergistically lethal with tra, possibly because photoreceptor differentiation has been a workhorse phenotype for the characterization of mutants in the Ras/ERK/ETS pathway (Nagaraj and Banerjee, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI network analysis of trametinib synergy data and citation to previous work on photoreceptor differentiation.

claim: The top scoring PPI network for rapamycin-synergy was one involved in the positive regulation of cell-size.
source: Similarly, the top scoring PPI network for RAP-synergy was one involved in the positive regulation of cell-size, a key morphological consequence of upgregulating the PI3K/mTOR pathway (Fingar and Blenis, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI network analysis of rapamycin synergy data and citation to previous work on PI3K/mTOR pathway effects.

claim: Similar PPI networks involved in mitosis were identified in both trametinib and rapamycin screens.
source: Interestingly, similar PPI networks involved in mitosis was identified in both screens (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI network analysis shown in Figure 4F comparing both drug screens.

claim: The use of lentiviral vectors in insect cells is extremely inefficient possibly due to toxicity.
source: However, the use of lentiviral vectors in insect cells is extremely inefficient (unpublished observations) possibly due to toxicity (Qin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished observations and citation to previous work on lentiviral toxicity in insect cells.

claim: A previous study attempted to use pooled transient transfection for barcoded delivery of a DNA library in Drosophila cells but failed to identify any essential genes using the system.
source: We note that a previous study attempted to use pooled transient transfection for barcoded delivery of a DNA library in Drosophila cells but failed to identify any essential genes using the system, most likely due to the lack of a mechanism for retention of the DNA reagents in the cells through extended passaging (Bassett et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the previous study and inference about the reason for failure.

claim: Approximately half of the genes in Drosophila lack functional characterization.
source: Approximately half of the genes in Drosophila, arguably the best characterized multicellular genetic model system, lack functional characterization (Ewen-Campen et al., 2017), so the need to develop orthogonal screening approaches is clear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on Drosophila gene characterization status.

claim: CRISPR generates complete loss-of-function alleles and causes fewer off-target effects on average compared to RNAi.
source: CRISPR generates complete loss-of-function alleles and causes fewer off-target effects on average (Morgens et al., 2016; Evers et al., 2016), and the pooled format allows greater multiplicity and replication for unit cost.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous comparative studies of CRISPR and RNAi.

claim: The pooled format allows greater multiplicity and replication for unit cost compared to arrayed formats.
source: CRISPR generates complete loss-of-function alleles and causes fewer off-target effects on average (Morgens et al., 2016; Evers et al., 2016), and the pooled format allows greater multiplicity and replication for unit cost.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the advantages of pooled versus arrayed screening formats.

claim: Essential genes are, by definition, a subset of fitness genes.
source: By comparing the abundance of guides present in actively growing populations of cells at different time points during growth, CRISPR screens provide a relative measurement of cell doubling, but because the cause of proliferation reduction is unclear from the screen alone, the screens are said to identify genes necessary for optimal fitness rather than essential genes (Hart et al., 2015). Essential genes, those absolutely required for cell doubling, are, by definition, a subset of fitness genes.
evidence: The claim is a definitional statement supported by citation to previous work on fitness gene terminology.

claim: RNAi was more likely to identify highly expressed genes, whereas this bias was less prominent in the CRISPR screen.
source: Among genes with an RPKM > 1, RNAi was more likely to identify highly expressed genes, whereas this bias was less prominent in the CRISPR screen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of expression level effects shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A human CRISPR-RNAi screen comparison found a similar inability of RNAi to detect genes of the mitochondrial ribosome whereas it exceeded CRISPR sensitivity in detecting genes of the cytoplasmic ribosome, possibly due to differences in mRNA stability.
source: Interestingly, a human CRISPR-RNAi screen comparison also found a similar inability of RNAi to detect genes of the mitochondrial ribosome whereas it exceeded CRISPR sensitivity in detecting genes of the cytoplasmic ribosome, possibly due to differences in mRNA stability (Hart et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a human screen comparison study and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The position matrix shows complementary nucleotide biases and is broadly consistent with human CRISPR screens, supporting an underlying mechanistic unity of targeting by Cas9 and NHEJ repair between human and fly cells.
source: The position matrix shows complementary nucleotide biases at 15/21 positions and is broadly consistent with human CRISPR screens (Doench et al., 2016). Specifically, out of the first position of the PAM sequence and the 8 bp seed region before the PAM sequence, 5 of 9 positions are fully consistent while 2 of 9 position are partially consistent with the Doench score (Doench et al., 2016) (Figure 2H). The analyses support an underlying mechanistic unity of targeting by Cas9 and NHEJ repair between human and fly cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity of position matrices between fly and human CRISPR screens.

claim: CNA genes in Drosophila cells are enriched for fitness essentiality.
source: Interestingly, genes with extreme CNA of 8 or more copies (3% of genes) exhibited a bias of ~1.8 fold in the CRISPR screen, but the magnitude of this bias was similar to that seen in an RNAi screen for the same genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that CNA genes in Drosophila cells are enriched for fitness essentiality.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both CRISPR and RNAi show similar biases for high CNA genes.

claim: Drosophila CRISPR screens do not have detectable copy-number bias.
source: The analysis shows that Drosophila CRISPR screens do not have detectable copy-number bias.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the CNA analysis showing no bias for 97% of the genome.

claim: The fitness gene set is enriched for essential processes such as translation, transcription, splicing, etc.
source: We first performed gene ontology enrichment on CRISPR screen hits at 5% FDR. The gene set is enriched for essential processes such as translation, transcription, splicing, etc. and depletion for processes such as chitin metabolism that are necessary in whole flies but not cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The fitness gene set is depleted for processes such as chitin metabolism that are necessary in whole flies but not cells.
source: We first performed gene ontology enrichment on CRISPR screen hits at 5% FDR. The gene set is enriched for essential processes such as translation, transcription, splicing, etc. and depletion for processes such as chitin metabolism that are necessary in whole flies but not cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The overlap between cell-essential and whole-fly essential genes may represent different genetic requirements of whole animals versus cell lines or of germline versus somatic cells.
source: This overlap is in a similar range as knockout mouse viability compared with mouse cell-line fitness essentiality (where the overlap is ~27%) (Bartha et al., 2018), and may represent different genetic requirements of whole animals versus cell lines or of germline versus somatic cells (Garcia-Bellido and Robbins, 1983).
evidence: The claim is speculative inference about the biological meaning of the partial overlap, with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Functional redundancy among closely related genes buffers each of them and makes them invisible in viability screens.
source: Thus, we propose that functional redundancy among closely related genes buffers each of them and makes them invisible in viability screens, and that Drosophila cells may be more appropriate for screening genes that expanded during the vertebrate lineage.
evidence: The claim is a proposed explanation for the paralog effect observed in human CRISPR screens.

claim: Drosophila cells may be more appropriate for screening genes that expanded during the vertebrate lineage.
source: Thus, we propose that functional redundancy among closely related genes buffers each of them and makes them invisible in viability screens, and that Drosophila cells may be more appropriate for screening genes that expanded during the vertebrate lineage.
evidence: The claim is a proposed application based on the paralog analysis showing better detection of such genes in fly screens.

claim: Further studies of the 251 conserved uncharacterized fitness genes are likely to provide new insights into conserved, cell essential processes not yet studied in flies.
source: Thus, further studies of these conserved genes are likely to provide new insights into conserved, cell essential processes not yet studied in flies.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about the potential value of studying these genes.

claim: Fly-specific fitness genes present a paradox and may reveal novel species-specific biology or overlooked structural/functional analogs without sequence orthology and may have potential as targets for new insecticides.
source: Also of interest are fly-specific fitness genes, as they present a paradox and may reveal novel species-specific biology or overlooked structural/functional analogs without sequence orthology and may have potential as targets for new insecticides.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about the potential biological significance and applications of fly-specific fitness genes.

claim: Characterization of the remaining conserved and non-conserved genes is likely to bring new insights into essential gene functions.
source: Characterization of the remaining conserved and non-conserved genes is likely to bring new insights into essential gene functions.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about the potential value of future research.

claim: CRISPR screening in Drosophila cells can reveal context-specific compensatory mechanisms or synergy relevant to major signaling pathways.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that CRISPR screening in Drosophila cells can reveal context-specific compensatory mechanisms or synergy relevant to major signaling pathways.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the drug screening results showing pathway-specific genetic interactions.

claim: The methods and constructs employed are likely to be directly transferable to the large number of existing cultured cell-lines derived from other insects such as mosquitos.
source: Finally, the methods and constructs we employ are likely to be directly transferable to the large number of existing cultured cell-lines derived from other insects such as mosquitos, where they could be used to characterize viral propagation mechanisms in the vectors of human pathogens such as Dengue or Zika.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about the potential transferability and applications of the method.

claim: The system should be amenable to adapting any pooled DNA library screening approach to Drosophila or other invertebrate cell lines, such as shRNA knockdown or CRISPR activation/inhibition.
source: The method should be amenable to adapting any pooled DNA library screening approach to Drosophila or other invertebrate cell lines, such as shRNA knockdown (Berns et al., 2004) or CRISPR activation/inhibition.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about the potential applications of the phiC31 integration method, with citation to shRNA knockdown.

claim: The pooled approach in mammalian cells has been used extensively to perform RNAi and more recently single guide RNA (sgRNA) screens using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: The pooled approach in mammalian cells has been used extensively to perform RNAi and more recently single guide RNA (sgRNA) screens using CRISPR/Cas9 (Shalem et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Hart et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous mammalian pooled screening studies.

claim: Genetic loss-of-function arrayed RNAi screens in Drosophila cell lines have provided insight into genes regulating various biological processes.
source: Genetic loss-of-function arrayed RNAi screens in Drosophila cell lines have provided insight into genes regulating various biological processes (Boutros et al., 2004; Björklund et al., 2006; Kiger et al., 2003; D'Ambrosio and Vale, 2010; Bard et al., 2006; Guo et al., 2008; Hao et al., 2008; Housden et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous Drosophila RNAi screening studies.

claim: Arrayed RNAi screening has drawbacks that limit resolution, including off-target effects and incomplete loss-of-function due to RNAi, and the high cost of reagent multiplicity and replication due to the arrayed format.
source: However, this approach has drawbacks that limit resolution, including off-target effects and incomplete loss-of-function due to RNAi, and the high cost of reagent multiplicity and replication due to the arrayed format.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the limitations of RNAi and arrayed screening formats.

claim: Pooled CRISPR may address the major drawbacks of arrayed RNAi: CRISPR generates complete loss-of-function alleles and causes fewer off-target effects on average, and the pooled format allows greater multiplicity and replication for unit cost.
source: Pooled CRISPR may address the major drawbacks: CRISPR generates complete loss-of-function alleles and causes fewer off-target effects on average (Morgens et al., 2016; Evers et al., 2016), and the pooled format allows greater multiplicity and replication for unit cost.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous comparative studies and general knowledge about pooled screening advantages.

claim: CRISPR screens provide a relative measurement of cell doubling by comparing the abundance of guides present in actively growing populations of cells at different time points during growth.
source: By comparing the abundance of guides present in actively growing populations of cells at different time points during growth, CRISPR screens provide a relative measurement of cell doubling, but because the cause of proliferation reduction is unclear from the screen alone, the screens are said to identify genes necessary for optimal fitness rather than essential genes (Hart et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about how CRISPR screens work, with citation to previous work on fitness gene terminology.

claim: CRISPR screens identify genes necessary for optimal fitness rather than essential genes because the cause of proliferation reduction is unclear from the screen alone.
source: By comparing the abundance of guides present in actively growing populations of cells at different time points during growth, CRISPR screens provide a relative measurement of cell doubling, but because the cause of proliferation reduction is unclear from the screen alone, the screens are said to identify genes necessary for optimal fitness rather than essential genes (Hart et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to previous work defining fitness genes versus essential genes.

claim: Both Ras/ERK/ETS and PI3K/mTor pathways are pro-survival pathways that have been extensively mapped through loss-of-function studies in fly tissues and cell-lines.
